warmup.q: Redis runs every command on one thread and takes no locks. Two pods handle purchases on the same prepaid card at the same moment, and each runs GET balance:7, subtracts in its own code, then SET balance:7 <new value>. Can a debit be lost?
options: No: with one thread, only one pod's code runs at a time
Yes: the thread runs each command alone, but other clients' commands can run between one pod's GET and its SET
No: Redis holds the key for a client between its GET and its next SET
Only if Redis I/O threads are switched on
warmup.why: One thread makes each command a transaction of its own, run start to finish with nothing in between. A GET and a later SET are two commands, so both pods can GET 100 before either SETs, and one debit disappears. Only what arrives as one unit runs alone, which is why serial engines want the whole transaction at once. Redis never holds a key for a client between commands, and I/O threads only read and write sockets: commands still run on one thread.

sections.h: Run transactions one at a time on one thread, and concurrency control disappears
sections.html:
Lessons 2 to 5 built a lot of machinery: row locks, lock queues, versions and snapshots, a deadlock detector, SIREAD notes. All of it exists because transactions run at the same time. Here is the blunt alternative: run them one at a time. One thread takes a transaction, runs it to the end, and only then takes the next. Every history is serial, so it is serializable by definition. No locks, no deadlocks, no serialization failures.

For decades nobody built databases this way, for two reasons. A transaction that waited 10 ms for a disk read left the only thread idle, so a database needed many transactions in flight to keep the CPU busy. And transactions were interactive: the application sends a statement, thinks, sends the next. Two things changed. Memory got cheap enough to hold the whole working set, so a transaction no longer waits for the disk. And OLTP transactions turned out to be tiny. In 2007, Michael Stonebraker's group at MIT noted that the heaviest TPC-C transaction reads about 200 records, under a millisecond of work in memory. Their prototype, H-Store, ran each partition of the data on one thread with no locking at all, and on the same dual-core machine it ran 70,416 TPC-C transactions per second against 850 for a tuned commercial database. H-Store became the product VoltDB. Redis also runs every command on one thread, as the Caching track's lesson on how Redis executes commands showed: its data is in memory and its commands are short.

Where does it break? The thread must never wait, and in an in-memory engine the slowest part of a transaction is the client. Say the engine needs 10 µs of work for a transfer, but the application drives it interactively: read the balance, decide in Kotlin, write and commit. That is two round trips of about 0.5 ms in one data center. If the engine keeps its thread for the transfer until it commits, the thread waits 1 ms for 10 µs of work, and the ceiling is about 1,000 transfers a second, however fast the CPU. If instead it serves other clients between the statements, the transfer is no longer isolated.

So serial engines want the whole transaction at once, as code they can run to the end without waiting: a stored procedure. VoltDB's procedures are Java classes; Redis's are Lua scripts. That is the model for this lesson: one thread, and each transaction arrives complete. The Try it measures what one Redis thread does when work arrives that way. The rest of the lesson uses Redis to answer the practical question: what can you send at once, and what happens to the parts you can't?

try.title: Measure what one thread can do
steps: From the labs folder, start Redis (docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d). redis-benchmark ships in the same image, so these commands run client and server in one container, over the loopback interface.

Run the four benchmarks below. The first uses one client that waits for each reply; the second 50 clients; the third 50 clients that each pipeline 16 commands; the fourth runs a whole transfer, read, check, debit and credit, as one Lua script per request.
Before each one, predict whether it is faster or slower than the one before, and by roughly how much.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.html: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli MSET acct:a 100000000 acct:b 0 docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -t set -n 20000 -c 1 docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -t set -n 200000 -c 50 docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -t set -n 1000000 -c 50 -P 16 docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -n 200000 -c 50 \ EVAL 'local b = tonumber(redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) or "0") if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call("DECRBY", KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) redis.call("INCRBY", KEYS[2], ARGV[1]) return 1' 2 acct:a acct:b 1

try.expect:
Two runs on the lab laptop (each benchmark prints progress lines, then this summary):

SET: 26881.72 requests per second, p50=0.039 msec        one client, waiting for each reply
SET: 227790.42 requests per second, p50=0.103 msec       50 clients
SET: 1848428.75 requests per second, p50=0.367 msec      50 clients, pipelines of 16
EVAL ... 2 acct:a acct:b 1: 193236.72 requests per second, p50=0.215 msec

The second run gave 26,525, 209,864, 1,886,793 and 187,441. One thread can run almost 1.9 million SETs a second, but a client that waits for each reply gets about 26,000, because the thread sits idle for most of every 39 µs round trip. The transfer script runs about 190,000 complete transactions a second on that one thread, with no locks and no retries. The numbers move with your CPU and with what else Docker is running; the ratios stay similar.

sections.h: Two commands from your service are two transactions
sections.html:
Redis treats each command as a transaction: one thread runs it to completion, with nothing in between. A sequence of commands from your service is not one transaction. Between your commands, the event loop (the loop from the Caching track that serves every client in turn) runs other clients' commands. In the terms of the first section, a sequence is an interactive transaction, and Redis chose to serve others while you think.

Here is the case that matters in payments. A prepaid card has 100 euros in balance:7. Two authorizations reach two pods at the same moment, 30 euros at a coffee shop and 50 at a fuel station. Each pod does what looks right:

Java
long balance = Long.parseLong(redis.get("balance:7"));
if (balance >= amount) redis.set("balance:7", String.valueOf(balance - amount));
Kotlin
val balance = redis.get("balance:7")!!.toLong()
if (balance >= amount) redis.set("balance:7", (balance - amount).toString())

Both GETs can run before either SET. Both pods read 100. One writes 70, the other 50, and the SET that runs last wins. The card has paid 80 euros and the balance shows 70 or 50. That is a lost update: one write overwrote another that it never saw. The simulator below lets you produce it: run both GETs first.

Why not one command? For an unconditional change there is one. DECRBY balance:7 30 reads, subtracts and writes inside a single command, so it can't lose an update. But a payment must not take the balance below zero, and DECRBY doesn't check: from 20, DECRBY balance:7 30 happily answers -10. The decision needs a read, a test and a write, with no other client's write in between.

One command runs alone; a sequence doesn't. Redis gives you three ways to send more at once. MULTI/EXEC sends a batch. WATCH checks a decision your code made from an earlier read. A Lua script sends the decision itself, the stored procedure of the first section.

sim.title: Two pods debit one prepaid balance
sim.intro: T1 and T2 are two pods. Each reads the balance, subtracts in its own memory, and writes the result back. 100 - 30 - 50 should leave 20. Can you end with 70?

goal.say: Lost update: the card paid 80 euros and the balance only went down by 30. Both pods read 100 before either wrote, and T1's SET overwrote T2's without ever seeing it.

try.title: Lose a debit by hand
steps: Open two redis-cli prompts in two terminals: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli from the labs folder (start the server first if needed).

Play the race: terminal 1 runs SET balance:7 100 and GET balance:7, terminal 2 runs GET balance:7, terminal 1 writes the coffee debit SET balance:7 70, terminal 2 writes the fuel debit SET balance:7 50. Then read the balance.
Now try the single-command version in either terminal: the last four commands. Predict the last answer.

code.title: two redis-cli prompts (the order to type them)
code.html:
SET balance:7 100
GET balance:7
GET balance:7
SET balance:7 70
SET balance:7 50
GET balance:7
SET balance:7 100
DECRBY balance:7 30
DECRBY balance:7 50
DECRBY balance:7 30

try.expect: Both GETs print "100", both SETs print OK, and the final GET balance:7 prints "50": 80 euros paid, 50 deducted. With DECRBY nothing is lost ((integer) 70, then (integer) 20), but the third debit happily answers (integer) -10. One command can't lose an update, and it also can't refuse to overdraw.

sections.h: MULTI/EXEC sends a batch at once, and WATCH checks a decision made in your code
sections.html:
The simplest way to send more at once is a batch. MULTI tells Redis to start queuing: every command after it answers QUEUED instead of running. EXEC then runs the whole queue as one step on the event loop, so no other client's command runs in the middle. That is a Redis transaction, and a transfer fits it:

MULTI
DECRBY acct:a 3000
INCRBY acct:b 3000
EXEC

No client can ever read acct:a debited and acct:b not yet credited. A batch has two limits. It can't decide: a GET inside MULTI also answers QUEUED, and its value arrives with all the other results at the end, too late to choose what to queue. And it never rolls back. A command Redis rejects while queuing, such as one with the wrong number of arguments, makes EXEC fail with EXECABORT, and nothing runs. But a command that fails while it runs, such as INCR on a key that holds a merchant name, fails alone, and the commands around it still run. In the words of the docs, "Redis does not support rollbacks of transactions". Coming from Oracle, read MULTI/EXEC as an atomic batch, not a unit of work.

For a decision your code makes, Redis offers a check instead of a lock. WATCH balance:7 notes that this connection depends on that key. You GET the balance, decide in your code that 100 is enough for 30, then send MULTI, SET balance:7 70, EXEC. If any client wrote balance:7 after your WATCH, even the same value again, EXEC runs nothing and answers nil, and you start over: watch, read, decide. It is the idea behind a JPA @Version column, check-and-set plus a retry loop, and the stepper replays the lost update with it. Redis never makes anyone wait; it refuses a decision made from a stale read.

Three details matter in code. WATCH belongs to a connection, so WATCH, MULTI and EXEC must go over the same one: Jedis's redis.transaction(false) holds one pooled connection and runs commands at once until you call multi(), while Lettuce shares a connection between callers, so a WATCH transaction needs a dedicated one. Watch only what your decision reads: the credit is an INCRBY, correct whatever the destination holds. And retries cost round trips, so on a key many pods write, most attempts lose. Redis 8 added one-command versions for a single key. SET balance:7 70 IFEQ 100 (8.4) writes only if the value is still 100, and INCREX balance:7 BYINT -30 LBOUND 0 (8.8) subtracts 30 only if the result stays at 0 or above. Neither helps when the decision spans two keys.

stepper.title: WATCH turns a lost update into a retry
stepper.intro: The same two debits as the simulator, now with WATCH.

frames.say: Both pods start the same way: WATCH balance:7, then GET balance:7, which returns 100. Redis records, per connection, which keys it watches. Each pod decides in its own code that 100 is enough: pod A plans to write 70, pod B plans to write 50.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 290" role="img" aria-label="Pod B's transaction runs and marks pod A's watch dirty"><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="180" height="196" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="110" y="42" text-anchor="middle">pod A (coffee, 30)</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="34" y="70" text-anchor="start">WATCH balance:7</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="34" y="94" text-anchor="start">GET balance:7 > 100</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="34" y="118" text-anchor="start">(computing 70)</text><rect class="box-ok" x="440" y="20" width="180" height="196" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="530" y="42" text-anchor="middle">pod B (fuel, 50)</text><text class="t-s t-code t-a" x="454" y="70" text-anchor="start">MULTI</text><text class="t-s t-code t-a" x="454" y="94" text-anchor="start">SET balance:7 50</text><text class="t-s t-code t-ok" x="454" y="118" text-anchor="start">EXEC > 1) OK</text><rect class="box-a" x="230" y="20" width="180" height="196" rx="8"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="320" y="42" text-anchor="middle">Redis</text><text class="t t-code t-a" x="320" y="72" text-anchor="middle">balance:7 = 50</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="320" y="98" text-anchor="middle">watched by A</text><text class="t-s t-bad" x="320" y="124" text-anchor="middle">A: dirty</text><text class="t-s t-ok" x="320" y="150" text-anchor="middle">B: done</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="232" width="600" height="46" rx="8"/><text class="t-s" x="320" y="260" text-anchor="middle">B's EXEC writes balance:7, and Redis marks every other connection watching it as dirty.</text></svg>
frames.say: Pod B is faster: MULTI, SET balance:7 50 (answers QUEUED), EXEC. Its watch is clean, so EXEC runs the SET and the balance is 50. Any write to a watched key, even one that writes the same value again, marks every connection watching that key as dirty. Pod A's watch is now dirty. Pod A doesn't know yet.

B's debit survives.</text></svg>
frames.say: Pod A sends MULTI, SET balance:7 70, EXEC. Without WATCH, this is where 50 became 70 and B's debit was lost. Now EXEC checks the flag first, finds it dirty, throws the queued SET away and answers (nil). EXEC also clears the connection's watches, whatever the outcome.

Both debits are in the balance.</text></svg>
frames.say: Nil means "you lost the race, start over". Pod A watches again, reads 50, checks that 30 still fits, and writes 20 in a new transaction. Nobody touched the key this time, so EXEC runs. The balance is 20: both debits counted. This loop is the lab's WatchTransfer.

On a hot key, attempts keep failing.</text></svg>
frames.say: WATCH is optimistic: it assumes conflicts are rare and pays only when one happens. On a key that 50 pods write all the time, most attempts lose, and each lost attempt cost several round trips. When one key is hot, send the decision to Redis as a script instead, which never needs to retry.

try.title: Watch a batch keep going, then make EXEC refuse
steps: Open two redis-cli prompts: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli in two terminals from the labs folder.
Terminal 1: run the first block, two batches. Before each EXEC, predict the results. The INCR targets a key that holds hello, and the second batch has an INCRBY with no amount.
Terminal 1: run the WATCH block up to the GET. Then in terminal 2 spend most of the money behind its back: DECRBY balance:7 8000. Back in terminal 1, run the rest and predict what EXEC answers.

code.title: terminal 1 (lines starting with # are notes)
code.html:
# two batches
SET acct:a 10000
SET acct:b 0
SET acct:note hello
MULTI
DECRBY acct:a 3000
INCR acct:note
INCRBY acct:b 3000
EXEC
MULTI
DECRBY acct:a 3000
INCRBY acct:b
EXEC
MGET acct:a acct:b
# check-and-set
SET balance:7 10000
WATCH balance:7
GET balance:7
# now switch to terminal 2 and run: DECRBY balance:7 8000
MULTI
DECRBY balance:7 3000
EXEC
GET balance:7
# Redis 8.4 and 8.8: one-command check-and-set
SET balance:7 7000 IFEQ 10000
SET balance:7 1000 IFEQ 2000
INCREX balance:7 BYINT -3000 LBOUND 0
GET balance:7

try.expect:
In the batches, each queued command answers QUEUED. The first EXEC prints 1) (integer) 7000, 2) (error) ERR value is not an integer or out of range and 3) (integer) 3000: the INCR failed alone, and the transfer around it still happened, so MGET shows "7000" and "3000". In the second transaction the bad INCRBY is rejected at once with (error) ERR wrong number of arguments for 'incrby' command, and EXEC answers (error) EXECABORT Transaction discarded because of previous errors. Nothing ran: MGET still shows 7000 and 3000.

Terminal 1's GET prints "10000", and terminal 2's DECRBY prints (integer) 2000. Terminal 1's EXEC prints (nil): the watched key changed, so the queued DECRBY never ran, and GET shows "2000", not -1000. SET balance:7 7000 IFEQ 10000 prints (nil) because the value is 2000, and SET balance:7 1000 IFEQ 2000 prints OK. INCREX balance:7 BYINT -3000 LBOUND 0 answers 1) (integer) 1000 and 2) (integer) 0: the debit would go below 0, so it applied nothing, and the balance stays "1000".

refs.title: Transactions: errors and why there is no rollback

sections.h: A Lua script is a stored procedure: the whole decision runs on the thread
sections.html:
WATCH tells you that you lost a race. A script removes the race, and it is the stored procedure of the first section: you send the logic to Redis, and Redis runs all of it on its one thread as one command.

EVAL takes the Lua source, the number of key names that follow, the keys, and then any other arguments. Inside the script they are KEYS[1], KEYS[2] and ARGV[1], and redis.call runs a Redis command and returns its result:

EVAL "local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
      if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
      redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
      redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[2], ARGV[1])
      return 1" 2 acct:a acct:b 3000

This lesson's model says what happens: the script runs from its first line to its last, and no other command runs in between. The read, the test and both writes happen together, with one round trip and no retries. Pass every key the script touches in KEYS, and don't build key names inside the script: Redis Cluster routes the call by its KEYS, as the last section shows.

The price is the other half of the model: one slow transaction stalls every client. Keep scripts short and bounded: a transfer, a rate-limit check, a compare-and-delete, never a loop over a big key. And a script doesn't roll back either. If it fails halfway, the writes before the failure stay, so check everything first and write last.

Sending the whole source on every call wastes bandwidth, so Redis keeps a script cache. SCRIPT LOAD returns the script's SHA1 digest, and EVALSHA <sha> ... runs the cached script. The cache is not durable. A restart, a failover to a replica or SCRIPT FLUSH empties it, and EVALSHA then fails with NOSCRIPT. Every client must catch that, load the script again and retry. Jedis throws JedisNoScriptException, and the lab handles it.

Redis 7.0 added functions for logic that should live with the data. FUNCTION LOAD installs a named library of Lua functions, and FCALL transfer 2 acct:a acct:b 1000 calls one. Redis saves libraries with the data and copies them to replicas, so they survive restarts and failovers. Use functions for server-side logic that several services share, and EVAL or EVALSHA for logic that ships with one service.

VoltDB asks one more thing of its procedures. It replicates by running the same procedure on every replica, so a procedure must be deterministic: the same input must produce the same writes everywhere, and the current time comes from VoltDB's own API, not the clock. Redis could replicate scripts that way until 7.0; now it always sends replicas the writes a script made instead.

try.title: Load, lose and reload a script
steps: At a redis-cli prompt, set two balances and load the transfer script. SCRIPT LOAD prints its SHA1 digest; the commands below already use it, because the same script text always gives the same digest.
Run the two EVALSHAs. Predict both answers: the second asks for 9,000 when 7,000 is left.
Run SCRIPT FLUSH (what a restart or failover does to the cache) and the same EVALSHA again. Then install the same logic as a function and call it with FCALL.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
SET acct:a 10000
SET acct:b 0
SCRIPT LOAD "local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0') if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) redis.call('INCRBY', KEYS[2], ARGV[1]) return 1"
EVALSHA 3ccbfe4f9ff6e5e06c85208eb88919f00da7b626 2 acct:a acct:b 3000
EVALSHA 3ccbfe4f9ff6e5e06c85208eb88919f00da7b626 2 acct:a acct:b 9000
SCRIPT FLUSH
EVALSHA 3ccbfe4f9ff6e5e06c85208eb88919f00da7b626 2 acct:a acct:b 3000
FUNCTION LOAD "#!lua name=ledger\nredis.register_function('transfer', function(keys, args) local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', keys[1]) or '0') if b < tonumber(args[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('DECRBY', keys[1], args[1]) redis.call('INCRBY', keys[2], args[1]) return 1 end)"
FCALL transfer 2 acct:a acct:b 1000
MGET acct:a acct:b
FUNCTION DELETE ledger

try.expect: SCRIPT LOAD prints "3ccbfe4f9ff6e5e06c85208eb88919f00da7b626". The first EVALSHA returns (integer) 1 (moved) and the second (integer) 0 (not enough money, nothing written). After SCRIPT FLUSH, the same EVALSHA fails with (error) NOSCRIPT No matching script. Please use EVAL. FUNCTION LOAD prints the library name, "ledger", FCALL returns (integer) 1, and MGET shows "6000" and "4000". FUNCTION DELETE prints OK. A function would still be there after a restart; a cached script would not.

sections.h: One thread per partition, and what crossing partitions costs
sections.html:
A serial engine has two limits, and the first section's Try it showed the first. One client that waits for each reply got about 26,000 SETs a second out of a thread that can run almost 1.9 million: the thread sat idle while each reply crossed the socket and the next request came back. Many clients at once fill the gaps, and so does pipelining: sending many commands without waiting for each reply, then reading all the replies. From the JVM, through Docker's network, 5,000 SETs one at a time took 1.1 to 1.6 seconds, and one Jedis pipeline took about 10 ms. Lettuce pipelines without being asked: its calls return at once, so 5,000 async calls are all in flight before the first reply, though by default it still flushes each command to the socket as you issue it.

A pipeline is not a transaction. Redis reads pipelined commands off the socket in chunks of up to 16 KB and serves other clients between chunks, so a pipelined DECRBY and INCRBY can be split by another client's read. One command's reply also can't shape the next command in the same pipeline. Use pipelines for bulk work whose commands you know in advance, and keep batches to around 10,000 commands, because Redis holds all the replies in memory until it can send them.

The second limit is one CPU core. To go past it, split the data into partitions and give each its own thread: H-Store ran one single-threaded partition per core, and VoltDB does the same. A transaction that touches one partition runs alone on that partition's thread, so throughput grows with cores and machines. A transaction that touches two partitions must run on both threads in lockstep, each waiting for the other. VoltDB reports about 1,000 cross-partition writes a second, orders of magnitude below its single-partition rate, and more machines don't raise it. So the data model decides the speed: a transfer between two wallets of one customer is fast if both live in one partition and slow if they don't.

Redis Cluster takes the strict line and has no cross-partition transactions at all. MULTI/EXEC, multi-key commands and scripts work only when every key hashes to the same slot, and otherwise fail with CROSSSLOT. Hash tags put related keys together: in {wallet:7}:main and {wallet:7}:hold only the part in braces is hashed. The Partitioning track covered how keys map to partitions, and the Caching track's lesson on Redis Cluster covers the slots. The next lesson is about the case serial engines avoid: committing one transaction on several machines.

try.title: Time 5,000 SETs three ways
steps: Run PipelineDemo (Java: Jedis and Lettuce futures) or PipelineDemoKt (Kotlin: Jedis and Lettuce coroutines) from the labs folder.
Predict the ratio between the first two lines before you look.
Run it twice. Which line moves most between runs, and what does that tell you about where the time goes?

code.title: PipelineDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.txn.l06.demo; import io.lettuce.core.RedisFuture; import io.lettuce.core.api.StatefulRedisConnection; import io.lettuce.core.api.async.RedisAsyncCommands; import redis.clients.jedis.AbstractPipeline; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** 5,000 SETs three ways: one round trip each, one Jedis pipeline, and Lettuce futures on one connection. */ public class PipelineDemo { static final int N = 5_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (RedisClient jedis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { for (int i = 0; i < 2_000; i++) jedis.set("warm:" + i, "1"); // warm up the JIT and the pool long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) jedis.set("acct:" + i, "100"); // send, wait, send, wait... report("one by one", t0); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (AbstractPipeline pipe = jedis.pipelined()) { for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) pipe.set("acct:" + i, "100"); // buffered, nothing waits pipe.sync(); // flush, then read all replies } report("one Jedis pipeline", t0); } io.lettuce.core.RedisClient lettuce = io.lettuce.core.RedisClient.create("redis://localhost:6379"); try (StatefulRedisConnection<String, String> conn = lettuce.connect()) { RedisAsyncCommands<String, String> redis = conn.async(); redis.set("warm", "1").get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<RedisFuture<String>> replies = new ArrayList<>(N); for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) replies.add(redis.set("acct:" + i, "100")); // each call returns at once for (RedisFuture<String> r : replies) r.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); report("Lettuce async, one connection", t0); } finally { lettuce.shutdown(); } } static void report(String label, long t0) { double ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6; System.out.printf("%-30s %8.1f ms %,10.0f SETs/s%n", label, ms, N / (ms / 1000)); } }

alt.title: PipelineDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.txn.l06.demo import io.lettuce.core.ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi import io.lettuce.core.api.coroutines import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient /** 5,000 SETs three ways: one round trip each, one Jedis pipeline, and Lettuce coroutines on one connection. */ private const val N = 5_000 private fun report(label: String, t0: Long) { val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 println("%-30s %8.1f ms %,10.0f SETs/s".format(label, ms, N / (ms / 1000))) } @OptIn(ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build().use { jedis -> repeat(2_000) { jedis.set("warm:$it", "1") } // warm up the JIT and the pool var t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(N) { jedis.set("acct:$it", "100") } // send, wait, send, wait... report("one by one", t0) t0 = System.nanoTime() jedis.pipelined().use { pipe -> repeat(N) { pipe.set("acct:$it", "100") } // buffered, nothing waits pipe.sync() // flush, then read all replies } report("one Jedis pipeline", t0) } val lettuce = io.lettuce.core.RedisClient.create("redis://localhost:6379") try { lettuce.connect().use { conn -> val redis = conn.coroutines() runBlocking { redis.set("warm", "1") val t0 = System.nanoTime() coroutineScope { repeat(N) { launch { redis.set("acct:$it", "100") } } // 5,000 coroutines, one socket } report("Lettuce coroutines, one conn", t0) } } } finally { lettuce.shutdown() } }

try.expect: Four runs on the lab laptop: one by one took 1,101 to 1,642 ms (3,000 to 4,500 SETs/s), one Jedis pipeline 8 to 11 ms (440,000 to 610,000 SETs/s), Lettuce async 147 to 159 ms and Lettuce coroutines 200 to 224 ms. The one-by-one line moves most, because it is almost all round trips through Docker's network, and those vary. The pipeline is 100 to 180 times faster with the same commands on the same server.

refs.title: Redis Cluster specification (hash slots, hash tags, multi-key operations)

analogy: Go back to the Caching track's bank branch with one very fast teller who finishes each request before taking the next. Two customers who each ask "what's my balance?" and later "set it to this" can overwrite each other, because other customers are served in between. A transaction is handing the teller an envelope of slips that she processes in one go, though if one slip is wrong she does the rest anyway. WATCH is asking her to refuse your envelope if anyone touched your account since you last looked. A Lua script is a written procedure she follows start to finish without looking up: a stored procedure. A second branch with its own teller is a partition, and a request that needs both tellers at once is the slow cross-partition case. Pipelining is passing a whole stack of slips through the window instead of walking back to the queue after each one. The analogy breaks on rollback: a real bank would reverse the whole envelope after an error, and Redis won't.
world: A prepaid card balance, a merchant's daily payout limit or a fraud rule's per-card counter are all read-test-write decisions, and all of them lose updates with GET then SET once two pods handle the same card. On Redis 8.8, a single-key debit with a floor is one INCREX ... LBOUND 0. Anything across two keys, such as moving money between a wallet and a hold, belongs in a Lua script or function, called with EVALSHA and a NOSCRIPT fallback. WATCH fits low-contention updates where the logic must stay in Kotlin, such as editing a merchant's configuration. Pipelines belong in bulk work: a Kafka consumer that applies a batch of 500 events can send their 500 writes in one pipeline instead of 500 round trips. If your Quarkus service uses a Lettuce-style shared connection, give WATCH transactions a dedicated connection. The design is already in your Kafka consumers: a consumer that owns a partition and applies its events one at a time needs no locks for that partition's accounts, which is serial execution per partition, and the pain starts when one event must change accounts in two partitions.
mistake: The most common mistake is reading MULTI/EXEC as a database transaction: code queues a debit and a credit, a runtime error hits one of them, and the developer expects nothing to have changed. Redis ran everything else, so money moved halfway. The second is treating a pipeline as atomic because the commands left the client together; other clients' commands run between them on the server. Both come from carrying Oracle's meaning of "transaction" over to Redis. Validate inputs before EXEC, use a Lua script when a decision depends on what you read, and use pipelines only for speed.

compare.title: A MULTI/EXEC transfer in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Transfer.java
java.html: // a transfer as one MULTI/EXEC batch; each queued command returns a Response try (AbstractTransaction tx = redis.multi()) { Response<Long> from = tx.decrBy("acct:a", 3_000); Response<Long> to = tx.incrBy("acct:b", 3_000); List<Object> results = tx.exec(); // both run here, nothing in between System.out.println(from.get() + " " + to.get()); // 7000 3000 }

kotlin.title: Transfer.kt
kotlin.html: // a transfer as one MULTI/EXEC batch; each queued command returns a Response redis.multi().use { tx -> val from: Response<Long> = tx.decrBy("acct:a", 3_000) val to: Response<Long> = tx.incrBy("acct:b", 3_000) val results: List<Any>? = tx.exec() // both run here, nothing in between println("${from.get()} ${to.get()}") // 7000 3000 }

compare.note: The commands on the wire are the same: MULTI, DECRBY, INCRBY, EXEC. Inside the block each call returns a Response that is empty until exec(); calling get() on it earlier throws, because Redis has only answered QUEUED. exec() returns null when a WATCH aborted the transaction, so Kotlin should type it List<Any>? and check. Java's try-with-resources and Kotlin's use both close the transaction object, which hands its connection back to the pool. Notice what neither version can do: look at the balance before deciding to debit. That needs WATCH or a script.

worked.title: Debit a prepaid card without going below zero

steps.say: The starting point loses updates: two pods can both read 100 and both write. The Caching track's lesson on how Redis executes commands showed the same pattern losing four increments in five.
steps.code: long balance = Long.parseLong(redis.get(key)); if (balance < amount) return false; redis.set(key, String.valueOf(balance - amount)); // another pod may have written since the GET return true;

alt.html: val balance = redis.get(key)!!.toLong() if (balance < amount) return false redis.set(key, (balance - amount).toString()) // another pod may have written since the GET return true

steps.say: Move the decision onto the server. The script reads, tests and writes inside one command, so nothing can run in between, and there is nothing to retry.
steps.code: static final String DEBIT = """ local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0') if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) return 1 """; boolean ok = Long.valueOf(1).equals(redis.eval(DEBIT, List.of(key), List.of(String.valueOf(amount))));

alt.html: val DEBIT = """ local b = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0') if b < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) return 1 """.trimIndent() val ok = redis.eval(DEBIT, listOf(key), listOf(amount.toString())) == 1L

steps.say: On Redis 8.8 the single-key case is one built-in command. INCREX ... BYINT -amount LBOUND 0 answers with the new value and the increment it applied; 0 applied means the debit was refused.
steps.code: List<Long> reply = redis.increx(key, -amount, IncrexParams.increxParams().lbound(0)); boolean ok = reply.get(1) != 0; // [new balance, applied amount]

alt.html: val (newBalance, applied) = redis.increx(key, -amount, IncrexParams.increxParams().lbound(0)) val ok = applied != 0L // [new balance, applied amount]

steps.say: Pick by the shape of the decision. One key and Redis 8.8: INCREX. Several keys, or Redis before 8.8 (or Valkey): a script, sent with EVALSHA and reloaded on NOSCRIPT. Logic that must stay in your service and rarely collides: WATCH with a retry loop. The lab builds the two general ones for a two-key transfer.

lab.title: A transfer with WATCH, the same transfer in Lua, and a pipelined bulk load
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 11 fail: five in WatchTransferTest and six in ScriptedLedgerTest, all against the shared Redis container. Balances are whole cents in plain string keys.

In WatchTransfer.java, write transfer as the javadoc describes: a loop of attempts, each with redis.transaction(false), watch, a read, multi, two queued commands and exec. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.txn.l06.WatchTransferTest'.

Read the test a change to the watched balance aborts EXEC .... Its hook spends 8,000 cents from another client between your read and your EXEC, exactly once. Your transfer must notice on attempt 1 and refuse on attempt 2.
In ScriptedLedger.kt, replace the TRANSFER placeholder with the Lua script, then write transfer with evalsha and a NOSCRIPT fallback, and openAccounts with one pipeline.
Run all 11 tests. Both 50-thread tests check that 2,000 random transfers neither create nor destroy a cent and never overdraw.
hints: tx.get(from).get() before tx.multi() returns the value at once. Treat a missing balance as 0.
After tx.multi(), tx.decrBy and tx.incrBy only queue. tx.exec() returns null when the watched key changed; go round the loop again.

Lua: local balance = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0'), compare with tonumber(ARGV[1]), then two redis.calls and return 1. Script numbers come back to Jedis as Long, so compare the result with 1L.
redis.evalsha(sha, listOf(from, to), listOf(amount.toString())). Catch redis.clients.jedis.exceptions.JedisNoScriptException, call redis.scriptLoad(TRANSFER) again, and retry once.

drill.title: The WATCH retry loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write transfer(from, to, amount) with Jedis's RedisClient: WATCH the source, read it, refuse an overdraft, queue DECRBY and INCRBY in MULTI, and retry when EXEC returns null. Then compare. Which key did you watch, and why not both?

answer.html: boolean transfer(String from, String to, long amount) { while (true) { try (AbstractTransaction tx = redis.transaction(false)) { // one connection, no MULTI yet tx.watch(from); String v = tx.get(from).get(); // runs now, on the watched connection long balance = v == null ? 0 : Long.parseLong(v); if (balance < amount) { tx.unwatch(); return false; } tx.multi(); tx.decrBy(from, amount); // queued tx.incrBy(to, amount); if (tx.exec() != null) return true; // null: 'from' changed, try again } } }

alt.html: fun transfer(from: String, to: String, amount: Long): Boolean { while (true) { redis.transaction(false).use { tx -> // one connection, no MULTI yet tx.watch(from) val balance = tx.get(from).get()?.toLong() ?: 0L // runs now, on the watched connection if (balance < amount) { tx.unwatch(); return false } tx.multi() tx.decrBy(from, amount) // queued tx.incrBy(to, amount) if (tx.exec() != null) return true // null: 'from' changed, try again } } }

recap: Serial execution: one thread runs each transaction to the end before the next, so every history is serial, with no locks, deadlocks or conflict aborts. It became practical once data fit in memory and OLTP transactions proved tiny: H-Store ran 70,416 TPC-C transactions a second against 850 for a commercial engine.

The thread must never wait for the client, so each transaction has to arrive complete, as a stored procedure. Redis runs each command, batch and script alone; a GET then a SET from your service are two transactions and lose updates.
MULTI/EXEC runs a queued batch with nothing in between. It can't branch on a read, and it never rolls back: a command that fails at run time fails alone.
WATCH makes EXEC abort if a watched key was written since, turning read-then-write into check-and-set with a retry. Redis 8.4 SET ... IFEQ and 8.8 INCREX ... LBOUND do it for one key in one command.
A Lua script is Redis's stored procedure: read, test and writes in one command. Cache it with SCRIPT LOAD, call it with EVALSHA, reload it on NOSCRIPT; functions (7.0) persist with the data.

The limits are one core (pipelining saves round trips but is not atomic) and cross-partition work: VoltDB runs it in lockstep at about 1,000 writes a second, and Redis Cluster refuses it with CROSSSLOT.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to protect a wallet debit (check the balance, then subtract) by sending the GET and the SET in one pipeline, "so they run together". Explain why that doesn't work and what you would use instead.
explain.answer: A pipeline only stops the client from waiting for each reply before sending the next command. Redis still runs the commands one by one, and it serves other clients between them, so another pod's write can land between our GET and our SET. Worse, in a pipeline we don't even have the GET's answer before the SET is sent, so the SET can't depend on it. Wrapping them in MULTI/EXEC doesn't help either, because queued commands can't use each other's results. The decision needs the read, the check and the write to happen with nothing in between. I'd use a short Lua script that reads the balance, refuses if it is too low, and decrements, called with EVALSHA and reloaded on NOSCRIPT. On Redis 8.8 a single-key debit with a floor is one command, INCREX key BYINT -amount LBOUND 0. WATCH with a retry loop also works, but on a busy wallet it retries a lot.

deeper.html:
Scripts declare what they do. A script can start with a shebang line, #!lua flags=no-writes, and Redis then knows it only reads: it may run on a replica, and it is allowed while the server is out of memory. Without flags, a script is treated as one that may write. Functions take the same flags through redis.register_function{function_name=..., callback=..., flags={'no-writes'}}, and FCALL_RO runs a read-only function on a replica.

Time inside a script is frozen. Since Redis 7.0, Redis takes the time once when a script starts, and every command inside it sees that moment: TIME returns the same value, and key expiry is judged against it. The ExpiryDemo in the Caching track's lesson on expiry relies on this: 500,000 SET ... PX 3000 calls in one script all got the same deadline. It is also why a busy loop that waits on TIME never ends.

Replication of scripts changed in Redis 7.0 too. Redis no longer sends the script itself to replicas; it sends the write commands the script produced (effects replication). That is why a script may now use random numbers and the current time freely: replicas never re-run it, so they can't compute something different.

Transactions and scripts are both checked against maxmemory before they start (the Caching track's lesson on memory). Once a script has written something, Redis lets it finish even if memory runs out, because stopping halfway would break its atomicity. The same rule makes a long script dangerous in a second way: SCRIPT KILL only works on a script that hasn't written yet.

Deterministic databases push serial execution further. Calvin (Thomson and colleagues, 2012) first agrees, across all partitions, on the order of the transactions' inputs, and then every partition runs them deterministically in that order, so no partition ever has to ask another whether to commit. The price is that a transaction must say up front which keys it will read and write: no interactive transactions, as in this lesson. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 8, puts serial execution, two-phase locking and SSI side by side.
